title: Passwordless token refresh permits impersonation of any user
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and then issues a newly signed token for the subject in the untrusted claims. An attacker can choose a known user ID, including the staff account, and obtain a valid token with that user's current database role.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with JSON {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOjN9."} returned 200 and a valid signed token for sub 3 (the seeded staff user). The code at auth.py:101 uses jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}) before loading the subject.

title: Authenticated users can read any order
description: The order detail route authenticates the caller but calls get_order(), which only checks whether the order exists. It never applies own_order() or otherwise compares customer_id with the caller, exposing order contents and refund history across accounts.
evidence: With Priya's valid bearer token, GET /orders/3 returned 200 and the seeded order belonging to Tom, including its items, prices, payment amount, and status. show_order() at orders.py:46-49 calls get_order(order_id) directly.

title: Authentication decorator fails open
description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) as a broad Exception, sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Handlers that use g.user then produce an unhandled 500, while handlers that do not use it execute without authentication. The gift-card balance endpoint therefore discloses card balances to unauthenticated callers.
evidence: GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 without Authorization returned 200 with the card balance. GET /account without Authorization reached the handler and returned 500 instead of 401. The unconditional return f(*args, **kwargs) after the except is at auth.py:55-59.

title: Client-controlled basket cookie is unsafe-deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained to data values. read_basket() passes attacker-controlled cookie bytes to pickle.loads(), allowing a crafted cookie to execute arbitrary Python code in the application process before the type check.
evidence: GET /basket invokes read_basket() and therefore pickle.loads() on the request's basket cookie at basket.py:15-23. A signed/encrypted server-side session or a JSON value with strict validation is required; the current base64 encoding provides no protection against a malicious pickle payload.

title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQLite LIKE expression. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose or manipulate the query's result set.
evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all 6 products, including products unrelated to the search. The query at products.py:40-42 concatenates q instead of using a bound parameter.

title: Review bodies are stored XSS
description: Review text is stored without HTML sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. Any authenticated user can publish markup or script that executes for every visitor of the product page.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as Priya with body <script>alert(1)</script> returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the same script inside the review body. The sink is {{ r.body|safe }} at product.html:13, and add_review() only checks length at products.py:83-91.

title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
description: When the provider status request times out, the checkout handler explicitly changes the status to paid and proceeds to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore lets an order be fulfilled without confirmation of payment.
evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at payments.py:39-42 sets status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then set the order to processing and paid_pence to total_pence. The documented reconciliation job does not exist in the repository, so the fail-open state is immediately committed.

title: Payment webhook signature does not cover the payment amount or status
description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id. A request with a valid signature for an order can change amount_pence independently, including setting paid_pence to zero or an amount greater than the order total, and the handler accepts it without provider-side verification.
evidence: webhook_signature() at payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id), while payment_webhook() at lines 69-71 trusts event.status and int(event.amount_pence) separately. The configured fallback secret is the hardcoded value whsec-local in config.py:8, making the signing key recoverable from the source/deployment defaults.

title: Approved-host image import can be redirected to internal URLs
description: The endpoint validates that the initial URL uses an approved public hostname, but requests.get() follows redirects by default. An approved host can redirect the server to localhost, private network addresses, or cloud metadata, turning this staff-accessible importer into SSRF.
evidence: check_url() at images.py:28-35 validates only the parsed initial URL and its DNS result. The subsequent requests.get(url, ...) at line 50 follows HTTP redirects without revalidating each destination. No redirect=False or per-hop destination check is present.

title: Cancellation and return refunds can overlap and exceed the purchase
description: Cancellation validation tracks only cancelled_qty, while return validation tracks only returned_qty. The same item quantity can therefore be cancelled and returned in separate requests, producing two refunds. Neither path checks the aggregate refund total against paid_pence, and concurrent requests can also pass their checks before either update commits.
evidence: cancel_items() validates item['cancelled_qty'] at orders.py:62-68 and issues a refund at lines 69-70; return_items() independently validates item['returned_qty'] at lines 88-94 and issues another refund at lines 95-96. There is no cross-check against the other quantity or existing refunds.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashes use a fast, unsalted general-purpose hash. A database disclosure permits efficient dictionary and brute-force cracking, and identical passwords are trivially identifiable across accounts. Passwords should use a memory-hard password KDF with a unique salt.
evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at auth.py:15-16, and the result is stored directly in users.password_hash during registration and reset. No salt or work factor is present.

title: Request logging records passwords and other secrets
description: All POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies are logged verbatim up to 2,000 characters. Login and registration bodies contain passwords; reset requests contain reset-related data; other logged bodies may contain payment or personal information. These secrets persist in application logs and may be accessible to operators or log aggregators.
evidence: The before_request hook at __init__.py:29-31 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs it without redaction. This applies to /auth/login, /auth/register, and /auth/reset/confirm as well as every other mutating route.
